transcript.en: A student's search runs in a blink on ten thousand records. On the university's ten million, it never finishes. Their code was correct. What did they miss? Today: what Big-O really says, why students confuse it with speed, and how to teach growth rates so they stick. Big-O describes how running time grows as the input grows. It ignores constant factors and small inputs. It is an upper bound, while Theta gives a tight bound and Omega a lower one. We write f of n is O of g of n when some constant c and some n zero exist with f at most c times g for every n beyond n zero. The definition is about the eventual shape of the curve. A loop inside a loop over n items does n squared steps. Halving the range each time, as binary search does, takes about log n steps. At ten million records, that is a hundred trillion steps against about twenty four. Divide-and-conquer algorithms give recurrences such as T of n equals two T of n over two plus n. The master theorem solves the common forms. Merge sort comes out at n log n. Students often think Big-O means seconds, or that O of n squared is always slower than O of n. Let them time two algorithms on growing inputs and plot the curves. Then introduce the definition to explain what they saw. Quick check! One algorithm takes one hundred n steps, another takes n squared. For large n, which is slower? The n squared one, once n passes one hundred. Below that, it is actually faster. Big-O tells you who wins in the end, not who wins on small inputs. In the app, open the Big-O lab. Grow the input and watch the step counts of different algorithms pull apart. Your turn. A student says linear search is O of n squared. Is that statement true? True, but not tight: O is only an upper bound, and Theta of n is the precise answer. Remember: Big-O is about growth, constants vanish, and recurrences solve divide and conquer. Try it in your next lecture: give pairs two sorting functions and inputs of one thousand to one million. They time both and plot the results. Then ask which curve matches n log n.

title.en: Growth rates and how to teach them

body.en:
Asymptotic notation describes how a function grows as its argument grows. Formally, f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c × g(n) for all n ≥ n₀; Ω gives the matching lower bound, and Θ holds when both do (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms). Constant factors and lower-order terms disappear, which is why 3n² + 10n + 7 = Θ(n²). Big-O therefore says nothing about seconds on a given machine, and nothing about small inputs.

Recursive algorithms produce recurrences. The master theorem solves T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) by comparing f(n) with n^(log_b a): merge sort, with a = b = 2 and f(n) = n, gives Θ(n log n), and binary search, T(n) = T(n/2) + 1, gives Θ(log n). Recursion trees make the same result visible and are often the better first explanation.

Students’ common errors are well documented: treating O as exact rather than an upper bound, equating O with running time in seconds, believing a lower-order algorithm is faster for every input, and adding the costs of nested loops instead of multiplying them. Measuring before defining helps: when students time two algorithms on growing inputs and plot the curves, the definition arrives as an explanation of what they saw rather than as notation to memorise.

transcript.en: Half the class submits a recursive factorial that crashes with a stack overflow. Their loop version worked perfectly. What do they not yet understand? Today: how recursion really executes, why induction proves it correct, and the mental models that stop students treating it as magic. A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance. It needs a base case that answers directly. And every call must move closer to that base case. Each call gets its own frame with its own parameters and local variables. Frames pile up until the base case returns. Then they unwind one by one, each finishing its own multiplication. The crashing version tested for n equal to one but was called with zero. Zero minus one never reaches one, so the frames never stop. Testing for n at most zero fixes it. Structural induction mirrors the code. Prove the base case returns the right answer. Then assume the smaller call is correct and show the current call is too. That is exactly the recursive leap of faith. Students often picture recursion as a loop, or believe the function somehow waits without memory. Act it out: each student is one frame, holding a card with their own n. Then trace on paper before running any code. Quick check! The fixed factorial is called with four. How many frames are on the stack at the deepest point? Five: fact of four, three, two, one and zero. Each holds its own n, waiting for the call below it to return. In the app, open the recursion lab. Step through the calls and watch frames push and pop on the stack. Your turn. In the induction proof for a recursive function, what do you assume in the inductive step? You assume the smaller recursive call returns the correct answer. Remember: every recursion needs a reachable base case, frames hold separate state, and induction is the proof. Try it in your next lecture: line up five students as stack frames for factorial of four. Each writes their n on a card and passes the result back up. Then the class writes the induction proof together.

body.en:
A recursive definition has base cases answered directly and recursive cases that reduce the problem to smaller instances. Termination requires a well-founded measure, such as n or the length of a list, that strictly decreases on every recursive call and is bounded below by a base case. Operationally, each call receives its own activation record on the call stack holding parameters, locals and a return address; frames accumulate until a base case returns, then unwind. Stack depth equals the depth of recursion, which is why a missing or unreachable base case ends in a stack overflow.

Correctness proofs follow the structure of the code. For a function on natural numbers, prove the base case directly; then, assuming the recursive call on a smaller input is correct (the inductive hypothesis), show the current call is correct. Structural induction generalises this to lists and trees. Teaching the proof alongside the code legitimises the so-called recursive leap of faith: students may trust the smaller call because induction justifies it.

Novices often hold non-viable models of recursion: a looping model that ignores separate frames, an active-only model that forgets the work done while unwinding, or a magic model with no mechanism at all (Kahney, 1983; Sorva, 2013). Physical role-play of frames, paper traces and visualisers address the mechanism; writing the proof addresses correctness. Assess both, for example by asking students to predict stack depth and to state the inductive hypothesis.

transcript.en: In week six of a programming course, a third of students say that after a equals b, changing b also changes a. They passed every coding quiz. How? Today: the hidden models students hold of how programs run, the research on novice misconceptions, and tracing activities that fix them. A notional machine is an idealised computer that explains how a language runs, at the level a learner needs. Students always build some mental model. Our job is to make sure it is a viable one. Sorva's review catalogues dozens of novice misconceptions. Assignment is seen as a lasting link. Variables are thought to hold several values at once. And students assume the computer understands what they meant. Here is a short trace. After three lines, a holds five and b holds seven. Students with the link model answer seven for both, and that wrong answer tells you exactly which model they hold. Research by Lister and colleagues suggests a sequence. Students who cannot trace code rarely explain it, and those who cannot explain it rarely write it. So assess tracing and explaining in plain English, not only writing. Draw memory as labelled boxes on the board for every lecture example. Use visualisers such as Python Tutor. And use multiple-choice tracing questions whose wrong options each match one known misconception. Quick check! b is five, then a equals b, then b becomes seven. What does print a, b show? Five and seven. Assignment copies the value at that moment. It does not create a lasting link between the two names. In the app, open the trace lab. Predict each variable after every line, then step through and compare your prediction with the machine. Your turn. A student answers seven, seven. Which misconception does that answer reveal? It reveals the belief that assignment creates a lasting link. Remember: every student holds a notional machine, tracing comes before writing, and wrong answers are diagnostic. Try it in your next lecture: start with three tracing questions, each with distractors that match a known misconception. Students vote on their phones. Then redraw memory for the question most students missed.

body.en:
Du Boulay (1986) introduced the notional machine: an idealised computer, tied to a language or paradigm, whose behaviour explains what programs do at a level suitable for learners. Students inevitably construct a mental model of program execution; the question is whether it is viable. Sorva’s (2013) review catalogues well over a hundred documented novice misconceptions, including assignment as a lasting link between variables, variables holding several values, the belief that the computer infers intent, and confusion between a function’s definition and its call.

The BRACElet and related studies (Lister et al., 2004; Lopez et al., 2008) found evidence of a rough hierarchy: students who cannot reliably trace code seldom explain its purpose in plain English, and those who cannot explain it seldom write correct code. Assessing only code writing therefore hides the cause of failure. Explain-in-plain-English questions and tracing questions are cheap, scalable and diagnostic.

Instruction should make the machine visible: draw memory consistently as labelled boxes, use program visualisers such as Python Tutor (Guo, 2013), and design multiple-choice tracing questions whose distractors each correspond to a specific misconception, so that wrong answers diagnose the model a student holds. Peer instruction on such questions (Porter et al., 2013) improves outcomes in introductory programming courses.
body.ar:
قدّم Du Boulay (١٩٨٦) مفهوم الآلة التصوّرية: حاسوب مثالي مرتبط بلغة أو نموذج برمجي، يفسّر سلوكه ما تفعله البرامج على مستوى يناسب المتعلمين. ويبني الطلاب حتمًا نموذجًا ذهنيًا لتنفيذ البرنامج، والسؤال هو هل هذا النموذج صالح. وتجمع مراجعة Sorva (٢٠١٣) أكثر من مئة تصوّر خاطئ موثّق لدى المبتدئين، منها اعتبار الإسناد رابطًا دائمًا بين المتغيرات، واحتواء المتغير قيمًا متعددة، والاعتقاد بأن الحاسوب يستنتج النية، والخلط بين تعريف الدالة واستدعائها.

ووجدت دراسات BRACElet وما يتصل بها (Lister وآخرون، ٢٠٠٤؛ Lopez وآخرون، ٢٠٠٨) أدلة على تسلسل تقريبي: فالطلاب الذين لا يتتبّعون الكود بثبات نادرًا ما يشرحون غرضه بلغة بسيطة، والذين لا يشرحونه نادرًا ما يكتبون كودًا صحيحًا. ولذلك يخفي تقييم كتابة الكود وحدها سبب الإخفاق. أما أسئلة الشرح بلغة بسيطة وأسئلة التتبّع فرخيصة وقابلة للتوسع وتشخيصية.

وينبغي أن يجعل التدريس الآلة مرئية: ارسم الذاكرة دائمًا صناديق موسومة، واستخدم أدوات عرض البرامج مثل ⁦Python Tutor (Guo⁩، ٢٠١٣)، وصمّم أسئلة تتبّع اختيار من متعدد يقابل كل خيار خاطئ فيها تصوّرًا محددًا، فتشخّص الإجابات الخاطئة النموذج الذي يحمله الطالب. ويحسّن التعلّم من الأقران على هذه الأسئلة (Porter وآخرون، ٢٠١٣) النتائج في مقررات البرمجة التمهيدية.

transcript.en: Four hundred students, one assignment, two teaching assistants. Last term the autograder passed code that only worked on the visible tests. How do you grade fairly at this scale? Today: how to design autograded programming assignments that measure understanding, how to find and teach bugs, and how to protect integrity when AI can write the code. An autograder runs each submission against a test suite and reports a score. It is fast and consistent. But it only measures what the tests check, so test design is assessment design. Give students visible tests for fast feedback. Keep hidden tests for edge cases such as empty input, duplicates and very large values. Code that hard-codes the visible answers then fails. This median passes the visible test but fails on even lengths. It always picks the middle element. A hidden test finds it, and the feedback message should name the case without giving the fix. Tests check correctness, not design or understanding. Combine an autograded part with a short code-reading task and a written explanation. Add a brief oral check for a random sample. AI assistants can now solve most introductory assignments. Detection tools are unreliable, so design for it instead. State clearly what help is allowed, weight in-person and explained work more, and ask students to modify or extend code live. Quick check! The median code passes the visible test. Which hidden test exposes its bug? A list with an even number of items, such as one, two, three, four. The correct median is two and a half, but the code returns three. In the app, open the bugs lab. Find the failing case in each short program and write the hint you would give a student. Your turn. Which assessment change best shows that a student understands code they submitted? Asking them to modify it live and explain the change. Remember: hidden tests catch shortcuts, feedback names the case, and understanding needs more than a passing score. Try it in your next lecture: show a submission that passes the visible tests and ask pairs to write one hidden test that breaks it. Collect the best tests and add them to next term's suite.

body.en:
Automated assessment of programming has a long history (Ala-Mutka, 2005; Keuning, Jeuring and Heeren, 2018). An autograder is only as valid as its test suite: if tests check a few typical inputs, submissions can pass while wrong on edge cases, or hard-code expected outputs. Good practice combines visible tests for rapid feedback with hidden tests covering boundaries, empty and degenerate inputs, large inputs for efficiency, and properties rather than single values. Mutation testing of the suite, by checking that deliberately broken reference solutions fail, measures its strength.

Feedback matters as much as the score. Messages that name the failing case without supplying the fix support learning, while unlimited resubmission with full test output encourages trial and error; limits or penalties on submissions are common responses. Debugging is a skill to teach explicitly, with hypotheses, minimal failing inputs and systematic tracing, rather than something students absorb.

Large language models can now solve most introductory programming assignments (Denny et al., 2024; Prather et al., 2023), and detection tools are unreliable and risk false accusations. Integrity is therefore protected mainly by design: a clear policy on permitted assistance, a larger weight on supervised and explained work, code-reading and modification tasks, brief oral checks for a sample of students, and software similarity tools such as MOSS (Schleimer, Wilkerson and Aiken, 2003) used as evidence for a conversation, never as a verdict.
body.ar:
للتقييم الآلي للبرمجة تاريخ طويل (Ala-Mutka، ٢٠٠٥؛ Keuning وJeuring وHeeren، ٢٠١٨). ولا تتجاوز صلاحية المصحّح الآلي صلاحية مجموعة اختباراته: فإذا فحصت الاختبارات مدخلات نمطية قليلة، أمكن أن تنجح تسليمات خاطئة في الحالات الطرفية، أو تحفظ المخرجات المتوقعة. والممارسة الجيدة تجمع اختبارات ظاهرة لرد فعل سريع مع اختبارات مخفية تغطي الحدود والمدخلات الفارغة والمنحلة والمدخلات الكبيرة للكفاءة، وخصائص لا قيمًا مفردة. ويقيس اختبار الطفرات لمجموعة الاختبارات، بالتحقق من أن حلولًا مرجعية معطوبة عمدًا تفشل، قوةَ المجموعة.

والرد مهم بقدر الدرجة. فالرسائل التي تسمّي الحالة الفاشلة دون تقديم الإصلاح تدعم التعلّم، أما إعادة التسليم غير المحدودة مع عرض كامل لمخرجات الاختبارات فتشجّع التجربة والخطأ، ومن الاستجابات الشائعة تحديد عدد التسليمات أو فرض جزاءات عليها. وتصحيح الأخطاء مهارة ينبغي تدريسها صراحة، بالفرضيات وأصغر مدخل فاشل والتتبّع المنهجي، لا شيئًا يمتصّه الطلاب تلقائيًا.

وتستطيع النماذج اللغوية الكبيرة الآن حل معظم تكليفات البرمجة التمهيدية (Denny وآخرون، ٢٠٢٤؛ Prather وآخرون، ٢٠٢٣)، وأدوات الكشف غير موثوقة وتنطوي على خطر الاتهام الخاطئ. ولذلك تُحمى النزاهة أساسًا بالتصميم: سياسة واضحة للمساعدة المسموح بها، ووزن أكبر للعمل المراقَب والمشروح، ومهام لقراءة الكود وتعديله، وفحوص شفهية قصيرة لعيّنة من الطلاب، وأدوات التشابه البرمجي مثل ⁦MOSS (Schleimer⁩ وWilkerson وAiken، ٢٠٠٣) تُستخدم دليلًا لبدء حوار لا حكمًا نهائيًا.

en: Vote (10 min): Show each question; students answer alone and commit to an answer.
Discuss (15 min): Where answers split, pairs argue for two minutes and vote again.
Explain (10 min): Work through the questions most students missed, showing the reasoning step by step.
Plan (5 min): Note which misconception to revisit next week and how.
ar: التصويت (١٠ دقائق): اعرض كل سؤال، ويجيب الطلاب منفردين ويلتزمون بإجابة.
النقاش (١٥ دقيقة): حيث تنقسم الإجابات، يتجادل كل زوجين دقيقتين ثم يصوّتان مرة أخرى.
الشرح (١٠ دقائق): حُلّ الأسئلة التي أخطأ فيها معظم الطلاب، مع عرض الاستدلال خطوة خطوة.
التخطيط (٥ دقائق): دوّن أيّ تصوّر خاطئ ستعود إليه الأسبوع القادم وكيف.
